candidates.title: Keep open sheets supported by their private folder
candidates.proposal:
Upgrade the prior single fixed-home folder route by closing its interruption gap: immediate return after reading does not cover being interrupted while sheets are loose. Each adult keeps their own neutrally labelled folder on the shelf, with instruction sets in closed, opaque, coded envelopes and a private code key inside. When consulting a set, the owner opens it over the folder and keeps every page resting inside the folder’s boundaries. Before stepping away, they put the pages into their envelope and close the folder. Only one set is open at a time. Return the folder to its shelf position after use; new sheets go directly into the owner’s folder.

The owner controls all filing and decisions about older instructions. This needs existing folders, envelopes, labels and a reading surface large enough to support the folder. If that surface is unavailable, the owner moves to a suitable private surface before opening papers. If papers spill or become mixed, the owner privately restores identifiable sets and asks the issuer about uncertain pages rather than guessing. Medication instructions and doses remain unchanged.

The mechanism prevents interruptions from leaving individual sheets behind. Compared with the original fixed-home rule, it adds a handling constraint but no index maintenance or scheduled searches. It assumes interruptions are a meaningful loss cause; its benefit is uncertain otherwise. Closed envelopes provide casual visual privacy, not protection against deliberate opening.
candidates.experiment: Each adult privately times retrieval of two sets and counts missing or misfiled sets before starting. Run for one month, then repeat the same retrievals and inspect their own filing. Share only seconds and counts, never document descriptions or diagnoses. At setup, rehearse one interruption using blank paper to check whether closing the folder contains every page. Record only the number of actual interruptions that left papers outside the folder and occasions when the reading arrangement was inconvenient. Stop the added handling rule if it causes spills or unwanted visibility; revert to the original closed-envelope, fixed-home arrangement. Retain it only if retrieval and misfiling results, together with interruption experience, justify the inconvenience.

candidates.title: Make locator changes recoverable
candidates.proposal:
Upgrade the prior private locator route where instruction sets genuinely need to remain in several existing folders. Preserve neutral folder and envelope codes, a private paper locator inside the owner’s closed envelope, and owner-only handling. Change the move procedure: before moving a set, its owner writes a temporary locator entry showing both its old address and intended new address. They then move the closed envelope, check its arrival, and cross out the old address. Until arrival is checked, both addresses remain valid places to search.

This closes the source route’s interruption gap: an instruction to update an address immediately does not make an interrupted move recoverable. On resuming an interrupted move, the owner checks those two locations and their own immediate work surface, completes the move, and resolves the entry. If the set remains missing, they mark it unavailable and contact the issuer for replacement instructions; they do not reconstruct advice. Each person alone controls their papers and any distinction between current and older instructions.

Resources are existing folders, envelopes, labels and the paper locator. This assumes multiple filing locations offer a real benefit and moves are infrequent. Compared with the original locator, it adds one short temporary entry per move while reducing reliance on remembering an unfinished update. If maintaining addresses is repeatedly skipped, the owner consolidates their envelopes into one fixed folder and retires the locator. Exterior codes and closed envelopes conceal content casually but do not prevent deliberate access.
candidates.experiment: Before setup, each owner privately times retrieval of two sets and counts misfilings. Rehearse a move with blank paper, stopping once before moving and once after moving but before confirming arrival; check that the two-address entry supports recovery. Trial for one month, then repeat retrieval timing and privately check every locator address against its envelope. Share only times, incorrect-address counts and missing or misfiled-set counts. Also record move-update effort without content details. Abandon the locator for a single fixed folder if unresolved entries accumulate or retrieval worsens without a compensating filing benefit. If no real moves occur, report that interruption recovery was rehearsed but its everyday benefit remains untested.

candidates.title: A limited reserve copy for frequently needed instructions
candidates.proposal:
Use redundancy for a small number of frequently needed instruction sets whose loss would otherwise leave the owner without the paper. At an already occurring contact with the issuing clinician or pharmacy, each adult may request an additional paper copy of the same instructions. Proceed only if the issuer can supply and identify it without a new visit or scanning service. The owner keeps the everyday copy in a neutrally labelled, closed envelope in their existing folder and the reserve in another closed envelope at a separate shelf position. A private note inside the folder records the reserve location and which issue it duplicates.

The mechanism preserves retrieval when one physical copy is misplaced; it does not prevent the original loss. If the everyday copy is missing, its owner retrieves the reserve, keeps it in the normal folder, and privately searches their usual paper-use locations once. On finding the original, the owner restores the reserve arrangement. Neither adult handles the other’s contents. When revised instructions arrive, the owner removes the former reserve from the retrieval position and asks the issuer about any uncertainty before treating another copy as current. No doses or clinician advice are changed.

This needs spare envelopes, shelf space, existing folders and issuer cooperation. Compared with one-copy storage, it can reduce time without accessible instructions but adds paper, maintenance and a risk of confusing versions. Limit it to sets the owner can reliably match. If an identical extra copy is unavailable or version matching is uncertain, use the single-copy fixed-folder arrangement. Envelopes provide visual privacy only.
candidates.experiment: Each owner records baseline retrieval seconds for selected sets and privately counts missing or misfiled papers. Trial for one month with at most two reserve sets per person. At setup, use blank-paper stand-ins to rehearse an unavailable everyday copy and a revision that invalidates the reserve; do not hide real instructions for testing. After one month, repeat ordinary retrieval timing, time reserve retrieval separately, and inspect both locations for misfiling and unmatched versions. Share only seconds and counts. Count actual misplaced originals even when reserves allowed retrieval. Stop the reserve arrangement at the first unresolved version mismatch, or if maintaining it is routinely skipped. With no actual loss, the trial establishes retrieval usability only, not a demonstrated reduction in disruption.
